content: Ketogenic diets (KDs), which are high in fat and low in carbohydrates, have been proposed as a potential treatment to reduce seizure frequency in individuals with epilepsy, particularly in children with drug-resistant epilepsy. This review updates previous evaluations of the efficacy of KDs, originally published in 2003 and last updated in 2018. To assess the effects of KDs on drug-resistant epilepsy, a systematic search was conducted in multiple databases, including the Cochrane Register of Studies and MEDLINE, up to April 2019. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-RCTs involving individuals of any age with drug-resistant epilepsy were included. The outcomes assessed included seizure freedom, seizure reduction (defined as a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency), adverse effects, cognitive and behavioral changes, quality of life, and attrition rates. Data were analyzed using meta-analyses, and results were presented as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The review identified 13 studies involving 932 participants, including 711 children (aged 4 months to 18 years) and 221 adults (aged 16 years and older). All studies were deemed to have a high risk of performance and detection bias due to the lack of blinding. The certainty of evidence for all outcomes was rated as low to very low. Ketogenic Diets vs. Usual Care in Children Seizure Freedom: Ketogenic diets were associated with a higher likelihood of seizure freedom compared to usual care (RR 3.16, 95% CI 1.20 to 8.35; P = 0.02; 4 studies, 385 participants). However, the certainty of this evidence was very low, making the accuracy of this estimate uncertain. Seizure Reduction: Ketogenic diets also showed a significant benefit in reducing seizure frequency by 50% or more compared to usual care (RR 5.80, 95% CI 3.48 to 9.65; P < 0.001; 4 studies, 385 participants). The certainty of this evidence was low. Adverse Effects: Commonly reported adverse effects included vomiting, constipation, and diarrhea in both the ketogenic diet and usual care groups. However, the true effect of these adverse events remains uncertain due to low-certainty evidence. Ketogenic Diets vs. Usual Care in Adults Seizure Freedom: No adult participants achieved seizure freedom in the studies reviewed. Seizure Reduction: Modified Atkins Diet (MAD) showed a potential benefit in reducing seizure frequency compared to usual care (RR 5.03, 95% CI 0.26 to 97.68; P = 0.29; 2 studies, 141 participants). However, the certainty of this evidence was very low, and the effect estimate is highly uncertain. Adverse Effects: Vomiting, constipation, and diarrhea were the most commonly reported adverse effects. One study reported a reduction in body mass index (BMI) and increased cholesterol levels in the MAD group, while another study noted weight loss. The true effects of these adverse events are uncertain. Ketogenic Diets vs. Ketogenic Diets in Children Seizure Freedom and Reduction: Up to 55% of children achieved seizure freedom with a classical 4:1 ketogenic diet after three months, and up to 85% experienced a reduction in seizure frequency. Modified Atkins Diet (MAD) resulted in seizure freedom in up to 25% of children and seizure reduction in up to 60%. A simplified MAD (sMAD) led to seizure freedom in 15% of children and seizure reduction in 56%. However, all evidence was of very low certainty, making the accuracy of these results questionable. Adverse Effects: Vomiting, constipation, and diarrhea were the most frequently reported adverse effects. Weight loss was noted in two studies, with one reporting more frequent weight loss and gastrointestinal disturbances in the 4:1 ketogenic diet compared to the 3:1 diet. Hypercalciuria was more common in children receiving the classical ketogenic diet compared to MAD. The true effects of these findings remain uncertain. Ketogenic Diets vs. Ketogenic Diets in Adults One study involving 80 adults compared MAD plus KetoCal to MAD alone. No adults achieved seizure freedom. At one month, seizure reduction was more common in the MAD-only group (42.5%) compared to the MAD plus KetoCal group (32.5%). However, by three months, only 10% of adults in both groups maintained seizure reduction. The certainty of this evidence was very low, and the results are highly uncertain. Adverse Effects: Constipation was more frequently reported in the MAD plus KetoCal group (17.5%) compared to the MAD-only group (5%). Diarrhea and changes in seizure patterns or semiology were also commonly reported (17.5% to 20% of participants). The true effects of these adverse events are uncertain. Authors' Conclusions The evidence suggests that ketogenic diets may be effective in reducing seizures in children with drug-resistant epilepsy. However, the evidence for their use in adults remains inconclusive. The studies reviewed were limited by small sample sizes, high risk of bias, and imprecision, resulting in low to very low certainty of evidence. Modified Atkins Diet (MAD) and other related diets may offer similar benefits to the classical ketogenic diet while potentially causing fewer adverse effects, but this requires further investigation. For individuals with drug-resistant epilepsy who are not candidates for surgical intervention, ketogenic diets remain a valid treatment option. Additional research, particularly in adults, is necessary to better understand the efficacy and safety of these diets.
